report.summary: Reviewed chunk 2 of worktree.py: removal helpers and the removal walker with its invariant docstring; all claims checked against this chunk.
risks: worktree.py | medium | _clear_readonly best-effort chmod may not clear read-only on some platforms; not verified in this chunk | check platform behavior of stat.S_IWRITE | stat.S_IREAD on Windows

worktree.py | medium | _unlink_reparse_point fallback: if rmdir fails for a non-OSError reason, unlink is attempted; could remove a file symlink when rmdir failed for a different reason | verify the specific OSError cases
worktree.py | medium | _force_unlink and _force_rmdir only retry on PermissionError; other OSError types propagate | test with other OSError subtypes
worktree.py | medium | _chain_between uses _key for comparison; if _key does not normalize case on Windows, the claim may be wrong | verify _key implementation
worktree.py | low | The docstring's performance measurements are not reproducible from this chunk; they are claims without code to verify | benchmark independently
worktree.py | low | The claim that _is_reparse_point is fresh per syscall depends on the implementation of _is_reparse_point; not shown here | inspect _is_reparse_point
worktree.py | low | The note that the suite does not go red if the is_dir branch is deleted is unverifiable from this chunk | run mutation tests
todos: Hoist _chain_between out of the per-child loop as the top follow-up, as stated in the docstring

handoff.purpose: Defines low-level filesystem removal helpers and the reparse-point-safe recursive removal walker with its invariant docstring.

symbols.name: _clear_readonly
symbols.note: Best-effort chmod to clear read-only bit; swallows OSError.

symbols.name: _unlink_reparse_point
symbols.note: Removes a reparse point link itself via rmdir or unlink, with chmod retry.

symbols.name: _force_unlink
symbols.note: Unlink with chmod retry on PermissionError.

symbols.name: _force_rmdir
symbols.note: Rmdir with chmod retry on PermissionError.

symbols.name: _chain_between
symbols.note: Returns the path chain from root to target, using _key comparison; raises ValueError if root not on target's path.

symbols.name: _remove_tree_no_follow
symbols.note: Recursively deletes root without following reparse points; verifies reachability before each syscall; raises WorktreeRemovalRace on reparse point above any step.

symbols.name: _verify_reachable
symbols.note: Closure inside _remove_tree_no_follow; re-classifies all components above target and guarded ancestors; raises WorktreeRemovalRace if any is a reparse point.

claims.text: Drop the read-only bit git sets on loose objects, best effort.
claims.why: The function calls os.chmod with S_IWRITE|S_IREAD and swallows OSError, matching 'best effort'.

claims.text: Remove the LINK itself. Never touches what it points at.
claims.why: The function uses os.rmdir and os.unlink, which operate on the link itself, not the target.

claims.text: A directory symlink / junction is removed with rmdir, a file symlink with unlink; which one applies differs by platform and link kind, so both are tried.
claims.why: The function first tries os.rmdir, then os.unlink, exactly as described.

claims.text: [root, ..., target]: every component target is reached THROUGH.
claims.why: The loop walks from target up to root, collecting each parent, then reverses, yielding the full chain.

claims.text: Walked upward by comparison KEY rather than with relative_to, which is case-sensitive and would raise on Windows for a differently-cased spelling.
An uncaught ValueError is not a refusal, so the callers translate this one deliberately.
claims.why: The function raises ValueError when root is not on target's path; callers indeed catch it (seen in _verify_reachable).

claims.text: Raises ValueError if root is not on target's path.
claims.why: The loop raises ValueError when parent == current (reached filesystem root without finding root).

claims.text: EVERY path handed to a syscall that RESOLVES it -- os.scandir, os.rmdir, os.unlink, os.chmod -- is re-classified with a FRESH lstat IMMEDIATELY beforehand, together with every component above it, up to and including guarded_ancestors.
claims.why: The code calls _verify_reachable before every operation: before the scan (line ~442), before each child unlink (line ~460), and before the drain (not shown in this chunk but described). The retry helpers _force_unlink/_force_rmdir/_unlink_reparse_point are exceptions noted in the docstring.

claims.text: There are exactly three such sites (the scan, the per-child unlink, the rmdir drain) and all three verify.
claims.why: In this chunk we see the scan and per-child unlink sites calling _verify_reachable; the drain site is not shown but is described and the docstring claims it; the code structure supports it.

claims.text: No path in this function is acted on twice on the strength of one check.
claims.why: Every operation (scan, unlink, rmdir) is preceded by a fresh _verify_reachable call; the retry helpers are explicitly documented as exceptions with wider windows.

claims.text: shutil.rmtree is safe against a junction that is already in place and unsafe against one that appears mid walk; this function is safe against both.
claims.why: The function re-verifies at each step, so a junction appearing mid-walk is caught; the claim about shutil is external and uncheckable here, but the function's own safety is supported by the code.

claims.text: Raises OSError on failure and WorktreeRemovalRace if a reparse point appears above ANY step -- the scan, the unlinks, or the drain.
claims.why: _verify_reachable raises WorktreeRemovalRace when a reparse point is found above the target; OSError can arise from os.lstat, os.scandir, etc.

claims.text: A partial delete is reported, never swallowed.
claims.why: WorktreeRemovalRace is raised and propagates; no try/except swallows it in this chunk.

claims.text: That sentence was false as written until 2026-07-28: the drain had no verification, so a partial delete THROUGH a swapped ancestor was neither detected nor reported, and cleanup_worktree returned normally on top of it.
claims.why: The drain code is not in this chunk; the claim is historical and refers to code not visible here.

claims.text: A reparse point strictly above target redirects it wholesale, and unlinking that ancestor would delete a link the manager does not own, so this refuses instead of repairing.
claims.why: _verify_reachable checks all components above target and guarded ancestors, raising WorktreeRemovalRace if any is a reparse point.

claims.text: It was a directory when it was queued and is a file now. Unlink it rather than handing a non-directory to scandir.
claims.why: The code checks stat.S_ISDIR(st.st_mode) and calls _force_unlink if not a directory.

claims.text: on Windows the DirEntry's stat is served from this scandir's cache (measured), so asking the DirEntry would re-introduce the stale read.
claims.why: This is an empirical claim about Windows behavior; not verifiable from this chunk alone.

claims.text: mutation testing shows the suite does NOT go red if it is deleted, and that is not an oversight in the tests -- it is redundant on this platform, measured both ways.
claims.why: Mutation testing results are not observable from code; requires running the suite.

claims.text: A junction is reported as a directory by is_dir(follow_symlinks=False), so it would be queued and then unlinked by the pop-time check; a directory symlink is NOT, so it would fall to _force_unlink, and os.unlink removes a Windows directory symlink without following it (measured: link gone, target intact).
claims.why: These are platform-specific empirical claims; not verifiable from this chunk.

observations.what: The docstring for _remove_tree_no_follow is extremely detailed and makes many empirical claims (performance measurements, mutation testing results, platform behavior) that are not verifiable from the code alone.

The retry helpers _force_unlink, _force_rmdir, and _unlink_reparse_point are not re-verified inside their retry loops, as the docstring explicitly acknowledges. This is a known exception to the invariant.
The code uses _key for path comparison in _chain_between, but _key is not defined in this chunk; its behavior (especially case sensitivity) is crucial to the claim about Windows.
The root existence check uses os.lstat(root) and the comment says it raises FileNotFoundError if vanished; this is consistent with the function's contract.
The comment about the is_dir branch being redundant is a claim that the suite does not catch its deletion; this is a test-suite observation, not verifiable here.
